newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament steps up anti-Yeltsin offensive.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament steps up anti-Yeltsin offensive.

text.p: Russia's lower house of parliament will on Wednesday discuss trying to force President Boris Yeltsin to step down because of ill health, although the Kremlin insists he is fit to rule.
Parliament's own legal department has already cast doubt over the motion, initiated by a leading opposition communist after Yeltsin was taken to hospital with pneumonia on January 8.
The legal experts have said it is not enough to dislodge the president, who has huge powers under Russia's constitution.
NTV commercial television said some deputies might try instead to simply appeal to the president, who turns 66 on February 1, to resign.
Yeltsin himself has not been seen since he went down with the disease, which struck just two weeks after he returned to the Kremlin after six months away for heart surgery.
But the Kremlin's chief doctor said that the president, who left hospital on Monday, went for his first stroll outdoors in two weeks on Tuesday and worked on papers for eight hours.
"He's in a completely satisfactory condition," Sergei Mironov told Reuters shortly after seeing Yeltsin at the president's Gorky-9 country residence outside Moscow.

"For the first time he went outside and went for a walk at his country residence. He went around the house...When we arrived he was talking to his youngest granddaughter. It was a lively conversation," he said.
"There are no medical indications, as of today, that suggest that Boris Nikolayevich will not be able to work as president of our country," Mironov earlier told U.S. cable network MSNBC.
But Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov said last year's election campaign and heart surgery and two heart attacks in 1985 meant that Yeltsin had not worked properly for two years.
"I am in favour of setting up a medical commission, carrying out exhaustive checks, passing a law on the transfer of power so as to put it all in a legal framework," Zyuganov told reporters.
He was speaking after laying a wreath at the tomb on Red Square of Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin, who died 73 years ago on Tuesday.
Zyuganov and other opposition politicians blame Yeltsin's absence for a host of problems dogging Russia, including long delays in state pension and wage payments.
On Wednesday the government is set to discuss the budget problem, which stems from a shortfall in tax revenues and has left millions of Russians struggling to survive the winter.
Presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais announced the sum he had paid in tax on Tuesday and called on other politicians to do the same.
He was responding to a decision by parliament to debate a new request to Yeltsin to investigate him for corruption.
Communist deputies accuse the 41-year-old market reform architect of earning money privately while in office, but Chubais denies the allegation.

Parliament also plans to target the Swiss diplomat who is overseeing post-war elections in Russia's breakaway Chechnya region on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
The chamber's international affairs committee has accused Tim Guldimann, head of OSCE's Chechnya mission, of violating the constitution by helping to fund the January 27 poll.
But in an interview with Reuters in the Chechen capital Grozny, Guldimann said on Tuesday he was doing nothing illegal.

"What we are doing here is helping to facilitate the holding of the election, as we did in Bosnia. Every step of our work has been fully coordinated with the Russian government...They were informed of everything and supported all of our efforts."
